claim: Two monkeys (Macaca mulatta) weighing 6.4 and 7.4 kg were trained in the study.
source: We trained two naive male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) in the study. They weighed 6.4 and 7.4 kg at the beginning of the experiment.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the subjects used in the study.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China).
evidence: Direct statement about institutional approval for the research.

claim: Rewards consisted of 1 to 8 drops of juice per trial (0.08 ~ 0.5 ml).
source: Rewards consisted of 1 to 8 drops of juice per trial (0.08 ~ 0.5 ml), with drop size controlled by a computer-controlled solenoid.
evidence: Direct description of the reward parameters used in the experimental task.

claim: Eye positions and pupil size measurements were monitored with an infrared oculometer system at a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
source: Eye positions and pupil size measurements were monitored with an infrared oculometer system at a sampling rate of 500 Hz (EyeLink 1000).
evidence: Direct statement about the equipment and sampling rate used for eye tracking.

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) has been shown to play an important role in representing the association between sensory stimuli and reward during value-based decision-making.
source: We focus our study on the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), which has been shown to play an important role in representing the association between sensory stimuli and reward during value-based decision-making (Wallis and Miller, 2003; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Rudebeck et al., 2013b; O'Neill and Schultz, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC receives visual sensory inputs from inferior temporal and perirhinal cortex, as well as from limbic structures including the amygdala and the cingulate cortex.
source: The OFC receives visual sensory inputs from inferior temporal and perirhinal cortex, as well as from limbic structures including the amygdala and the cingulate cortex, allowing it to have the information for establishing the association between visual information and reward (Carmichael and Price, 1995b, 1995a).
evidence: Statement about anatomical connectivity supported by citations.

claim: A significant number of OFC neurons encode the reward value associated with sensory stimuli.
source: Studies have shown that a significant number of OFC neurons encode the reward value associated with sensory stimuli (Wallis and Miller, 2003; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OFC neurons are typically reported to be insensitive to stimulus locations.
source: OFC neurons are typically reported to be insensitive to stimulus locations (Wallis and Miller, 2003; Kennerley and Wallis, 2009; Grattan and Glimcher, 2014).
evidence: Statement about OFC neuron properties supported by multiple citations.

claim: The value encoding in the OFC is affected by gaze location.
source: It has been reported that the value encoding in the OFC is affected by gaze location (McGinty et al., 2016) and OFC activities alternated between states during decision making (Rich and Wallis, 2016), which led to the suggestion that the value information may be processed sequentially, possibly guided by eye movements or overt attention.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: OFC activities alternated between states during decision making.
source: It has been reported that the value encoding in the OFC is affected by gaze location (McGinty et al., 2016) and OFC activities alternated between states during decision making (Rich and Wallis, 2016), which led to the suggestion that the value information may be processed sequentially, possibly guided by eye movements or overt attention.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Rich and Wallis, 2016.

claim: Similar visual perturbation manipulations have been shown to affect both monkeys' behavior and neural responses in the lateral intraparietal area that could be attributed to a bottom-up attention mechanism.
source: Similar manipulations have been shown to affect both monkeys' behavior and neural responses in the lateral intraparietal area that could be attributed to a bottom-up attention mechanism (Balan and Gottlieb, 2006).
evidence: Statement about effects of similar manipulations supported by citation.

claim: Both monkeys showed pupil dilation patterns clearly indicating they understood the reward association in single-cue conditions.
source: Although the dynamics of pupil responses during the cue presentation period differed between the two monkeys, both monkeys showed pupil dilation patterns clearly indicating they understood the reward association (Figure 2AB).
evidence: Statement based on pupil dilation data shown in Figure 2AB.

claim: Pupil size increased for both monkeys when the reward associated with the cue was larger (p<<0.001 for both monkeys).
source: A linear regression showed that the pupil size increased for both monkeys during the analysis time window when the reward associated with the cue was larger (p<<0.001 for both monkeys).
evidence: Statistical analysis of pupil size data with reported p-values.

claim: In double-cue conditions, pupil responses were dominated by the cue that predicted a larger reward.
source: Next, we looked at the pupil dilation pattern in the double-cue conditions. The pupil responses were dominated by the cue that predicted a larger reward.
evidence: Statement based on analysis of pupil dilation data in double-cue conditions.

claim: When cue combinations with the same higher value cue were pooled, the pupil dilation was similar to the condition when the higher value cue was presented alone.
source: When we pooled the cue combinations in which the cue with the larger reward was the same, the pupil dilation was similar to the condition when the higher value cue was presented alone (Figure 2CD, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1, Table 2).
evidence: Statement based on pooled pupil dilation data shown in figures.

claim: The pupil dilation did not reflect either the sum of the cue values or the expected value in double-cue conditions.
source: Nevertheless, the pupil dilation did not reflect either the sum of the cue values or the expected value, which was the mean of the two.
evidence: Statement based on analysis of pupil dilation patterns.

claim: The pupil dilation responses suggested that the monkeys understood the cue-reward associations under the passive viewing condition.
source: Overall, the pupil dilation responses suggested that the monkeys understood the cue-reward associations under the passive viewing condition.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pupil dilation data.

claim: A total of 846 neurons were recorded from Walker's areas 11 and 13, between the lateral and medial orbital sulci.
source: We recorded from a total of 846 neurons in Walker's areas 11 and 13 (Walker, 1940), between the lateral and medial orbital sulci (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct statement about the number and location of recorded neurons.

claim: Among 846 neurons, 232 neurons exhibited significant responses during the cue period.
source: Among the 846 neurons, we identified 232 neurons that exhibited significant responses during the cue period.
evidence: Direct statement about the number of responsive neurons.

claim: 110 neurons were found to be selective for reward value.
source: Among them, 110 neurons were found to be selective for reward value (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement about the number of value-selective neurons, with reference to Table 1.

claim: An example value-selective OFC neuron's responses were modulated by the value associated with the cue in single-cue conditions.
source: An example value-selective OFC neuron is shown in Figure 3. In the single-cue conditions, its responses were modulated by the value associated with the cue (Figure 3AB).
evidence: Description of example neuron data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When two cues were presented together, the example neuron's response pattern mimicked the pattern of pupil responses.
source: Moreover, when we presented two cues together, the neuron's response pattern mimicked the pattern of pupil responses (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of neural and pupil response patterns shown in figures.

claim: The example neuron's responses to single- and double-cue conditions were similar (two-way ANOVA, p<1e-7 for reward value, 0.16 for number of cues).
source: The responses to the single- and double-cue conditions were similar (two-way ANOVA, p<1e-7 for reward value, 0.16 for number of cues).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-values from ANOVA.

claim: For the example neuron, only the higher value cue affected the neuron's responses (p=3.06e-7 for higher value and 0.51 for lower value).
source: A linear regression further revealed that only the higher value cue affected the neuron's responses (p=3.06e-7 for higher value and 0.51 for lower value).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-values from linear regression.

claim: 73 positively tuned neurons showed greater responses when cues with larger rewards were presented.
source: The 73 positively tuned neurons showed greater responses when cues with larger rewards were presented, and the 37 negatively tuned neurons showed greater responses when cues with smaller rewards were presented (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement about neuron classification with reference to Table 1.

claim: 37 negatively tuned neurons showed greater responses when cues with smaller rewards were presented.
source: The 73 positively tuned neurons showed greater responses when cues with larger rewards were presented, and the 37 negatively tuned neurons showed greater responses when cues with smaller rewards were presented (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement about neuron classification with reference to Table 1.

claim: The two-way ANOVA showed the number of cues did not affect the population responses of positively tuned neurons (p=0.50).
source: The two-way ANOVA showed the number of cues did not affect the population responses of each group (p=0.50 for the positively tuned neurons, 0.29 for the negatively tuned neurons).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from ANOVA.

claim: The two-way ANOVA showed the number of cues did not affect the population responses of negatively tuned neurons (p=0.29).
source: The two-way ANOVA showed the number of cues did not affect the population responses of each group (p=0.50 for the positively tuned neurons, 0.29 for the negatively tuned neurons).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from ANOVA.

claim: Linear regression showed that only the higher value affected the responses significantly for positively tuned neurons (higher value: p<1e-7; lower value: p=0.70).
source: The linear regression of the population response on the values of both cues showed that only the higher value affected the responses significantly (higher value: p<1e-7 for both groups; lower value: p=0.70 for the positively tuned group and 0.14 for the negatively tuned group).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-values from linear regression.

claim: Linear regression showed that only the higher value affected the responses significantly for negatively tuned neurons (higher value: p<1e-7; lower value: p=0.14).
source: The linear regression of the population response on the values of both cues showed that only the higher value affected the responses significantly (higher value: p<1e-7 for both groups; lower value: p=0.70 for the positively tuned group and 0.14 for the negatively tuned group).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-values from linear regression.

claim: The mean responses between single- and double-cue conditions were not significantly different for positively tuned neurons (p=0.12).
source: The mean responses between the two conditions were not significantly different (two-tailed t-test, p=0.12 and 0.27 for the positively and the negatively tuned neurons).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from t-test.

claim: The mean responses between single- and double-cue conditions were not significantly different for negatively tuned neurons (p=0.27).
source: The mean responses between the two conditions were not significantly different (two-tailed t-test, p=0.12 and 0.27 for the positively and the negatively tuned neurons).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from t-test.

claim: The value-encoding OFC neurons' responses were highly homogenous and dominated by the higher value cue when multiple cues were presented simultaneously.
source: These results suggested that the value-encoding OFC neurons' responses were highly homogenous and dominated by the higher value cue when multiple cues were presented simultaneously.
evidence: Summary statement based on the preceding data analyses.

claim: For negatively tuned neurons, the dominating cue was the non-preferred cue.
source: Note that, for the negatively tuned neurons, the dominating cue was the non-preferred cue.
evidence: Logical inference from the definition of negatively tuned neurons and the observation that higher value cues dominate.

claim: The perturbation was a transient rotation of one of the cues that lasted only 100 ms.
source: The perturbation we introduced was a transient rotation of one of the cues that lasted only 100 ms.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The perturbation was independent of the assignment of the rewarded cue.
source: It was independent of the assignment of the rewarded cue, and the monkey would not gain any behavioral advantage, knowledge, or additional reward by paying attention to it.
evidence: Direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Visual perturbations induced no changes in pupil size.
source: Indeed, we observed no behavior indications that the monkeys were responding to the perturbations. They induced no changes in pupil size, and the monkeys' eyes were not attracted toward the perturbed location (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement based on pupil size data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The monkeys' eyes were not attracted toward the perturbed location.
source: Indeed, we observed no behavior indications that the monkeys were responding to the perturbations. They induced no changes in pupil size, and the monkeys' eyes were not attracted toward the perturbed location (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Statement based on eye position data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Visual perturbations affected OFC neurons' responses.
source: However, these subtle visual perturbations affected OFC neurons' responses.
evidence: Statement introducing the neural response data to perturbations.

claim: For positively tuned neurons, responses were significantly larger when the cue with higher value was rotated than when the cue with lower value was rotated.
source: For the positively tuned neurons, their responses were significantly larger when the cue with higher value was rotated than when the cue with lower value was rotated (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement based on neural response data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Among 73 positively tuned neurons, 28 (36.4%) showed significantly larger responses when the higher value cue was rotated than when the lower value cue was rotated.
source: Among 73 positively tuned neurons, 28 of them (36.4%) showed significant larger responses when the higher value cue was rotated than when the lower value cue was rotated.
evidence: Direct statement about the proportion of neurons showing significant effects.

claim: The mean responses to the higher and lower value cue conditions were significantly different for positively tuned neurons (mean difference = 0.28, p=1.31e-4).
source: The mean responses to the higher and lower value cue conditions were significantly different (mean difference = 0.28, p=1.31e-4, two-tailed t-test) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported mean difference and p-value.

claim: Only one positively tuned neuron (1.3%) showed significantly lower responses when the higher value cue was rotated.
source: Only one neuron (1.3%) showed significant lower responses when the higher value cue was rotated.
evidence: Direct statement about the proportion of neurons showing opposite effects.

claim: For negatively tuned neurons, responses were significantly lower when the cue with higher value was rotated than when the cue with lower value was rotated.
source: A similar but opposite pattern was observed in the negatively tuned neurons. Consistent with their tuning, their responses were significantly lower when the cue with higher value was rotated than when the cue with lower value was rotated (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statement based on neural response data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 12 of 37 negatively tuned neurons (32.4%) showed a significant increase of responses when the lower value cue was rotated.
source: 12 of 37 (32.4%) showed a significant increase of responses when the lower value cue was rotated (Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct statement about the proportion of neurons showing significant effects.

claim: Only 2 negatively tuned neurons (5.4%) showed a response suppression.
source: Only 2 (5.4%) neurons showed a response suppression.
evidence: Direct statement about the proportion of neurons showing opposite effects.

claim: The mean responses to the higher and lower value cue conditions were significantly different for negatively tuned neurons (mean difference = −0.39, p=8.05e-6).
source: The mean responses to the higher and lower value cue conditions were significantly different (mean difference = −0.39, p=8.05e-6, two-tailed t-test) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported mean difference and p-value.

claim: The difference between the responses to the higher and the lower value cue rotation conditions was not significantly different between the two monkeys for positively tuned neurons (p=0.17).
source: The difference between the responses to the higher and the lower value cue rotation conditions was not significantly different between the two monkeys (two-tailed t-test, p=0.17 for positively tuned neurons and 0.17 for negatively tuned neurons, see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical comparison between monkeys with reported p-value.

claim: The difference between the responses to the higher and the lower value cue rotation conditions was not significantly different between the two monkeys for negatively tuned neurons (p=0.17).
source: The difference between the responses to the higher and the lower value cue rotation conditions was not significantly different between the two monkeys (two-tailed t-test, p=0.17 for positively tuned neurons and 0.17 for negatively tuned neurons, see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical comparison between monkeys with reported p-value.

claim: The mean modulation index for the positively tuned neurons was 0.05.
source: The mean modulation index for the positively and negatively tuned neurons were 0.05 and −0.07, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of calculated modulation index.

claim: The mean modulation index for the negatively tuned neurons was −0.07.
source: The mean modulation index for the positively and negatively tuned neurons were 0.05 and −0.07, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of calculated modulation index.

claim: For neurons that showed significant attentional modulation, the mean modulation index was 0.13 for positively tuned neurons and −0.15 for negatively tuned neurons.
source: They were 0.13 and −0.15 for the neurons that showed significant attentional modulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of calculated modulation indices for significant neurons.

claim: When comparing neurons' responses with no perturbations and when perturbations were applied to the higher value cue, no significant change in the neurons' responses was observed (p=0.82 for positively tuned neurons and 0.21 for negatively tuned neurons).
source: Indeed, when we compared the neurons' responses when there were no perturbations and when the perturbations were applied to the higher value cue, we observed no significant change in the neurons' responses (Figure 4EF. p=0.82 and 0.21 for the positively and the negatively tuned neurons, respectively. See also Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Statistical comparison with reported p-values.

claim: Visual perturbations by themselves did not affect OFC neurons' responses.
source: Therefore, visual perturbations by themselves did not affect OFC neurons' responses.
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of responses with and without perturbations to higher value cues.

claim: The attentional modulation observed when perturbations were applied to the lower value cue was due to the attention shift toward the lower value cue.
source: The attentional modulation that we observed when the perturbations were applied to the lower value cue was due to the attention shift toward the lower value cue.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of neural responses to perturbations.

claim: When the visual perturbation was applied to the cue with less reward in the 8-drops condition, there was a decrease of responses among the positively tuned neurons (p=6.10e-7).
source: When the visual perturbation was applied to the cue with less reward (red dashed lines in Figure 5AC, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for individual monkeys), we saw a decrease of responses among the positively tuned neurons (p=6.10e-7, two-tailed paired t-test), and an increase of responses among the negatively tuned neurons (p=2.30e-5, paired two-tailed t-test), so that the population responses were driven toward the single cue conditions when only the lower value cue was presented (black solid lines in Figure 5AC, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for individual monkeys).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from paired t-test.

claim: When the visual perturbation was applied to the cue with less reward in the 8-drops condition, there was an increase of responses among the negatively tuned neurons (p=2.30e-5).
source: When the visual perturbation was applied to the cue with less reward (red dashed lines in Figure 5AC, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for individual monkeys), we saw a decrease of responses among the positively tuned neurons (p=6.10e-7, two-tailed paired t-test), and an increase of responses among the negatively tuned neurons (p=2.30e-5, paired two-tailed t-test), so that the population responses were driven toward the single cue conditions when only the lower value cue was presented (black solid lines in Figure 5AC, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for individual monkeys).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from paired t-test.

claim: When the 0-drops-of-juice cue was paired with another cue, the OFC neurons' responses reflected the value of the other cue (p=0.0097 for positively tuned neurons and 0.0077 for negatively tuned neurons).
source: By default, the monkeys' attention was away from the cue with 0 drops of juice, and the OFC neurons' responses reflected the value of the other cue (p=0.0097 and 0.0077 for the positively and the negatively tuned neurons, respectively, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni multiple comparison correction; blue solid lines in Figure 5BD, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for individual monkeys).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-values from ANOVA.

claim: When the visual perturbation was applied to the 0-drops-of-juice cue, there was a decrease of responses among the positively tuned neurons (p=2.73e-5).
source: When the visual perturbation was applied to the 0-drops-of-juice cue, we saw a decrease of responses among the positively tuned neurons, and an increase of responses among the negatively tuned neurons (p=2.73e-5 and 3.67e-4 for the positively and the negatively tuned neurons, respectively, paired two-tailed t-test; blue dashed lines in Figure 5BD, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for individual monkeys), so that the population responses were driven toward the condition when only 0-drops-of-juice cue was presented alone (black dashed lines in Figure 5BD, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for individual monkeys).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from paired t-test.

claim: When the visual perturbation was applied to the 0-drops-of-juice cue, there was an increase of responses among the negatively tuned neurons (p=3.67e-4).
source: When the visual perturbation was applied to the 0-drops-of-juice cue, we saw a decrease of responses among the positively tuned neurons, and an increase of responses among the negatively tuned neurons (p=2.73e-5 and 3.67e-4 for the positively and the negatively tuned neurons, respectively, paired two-tailed t-test; blue dashed lines in Figure 5BD, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for individual monkeys), so that the population responses were driven toward the condition when only 0-drops-of-juice cue was presented alone (black dashed lines in Figure 5BD, and also in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for individual monkeys).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported p-value from paired t-test.

claim: The normalization model explained 82.4% (s.e.m. = 1.46%) of the variance of the neuronal responses under the double-cue conditions with attention shifts caused by visual perturbations.
source: The model prediction matched the experimental data well. It explained 82.4% (s.e.m. = 1.46%) of the variance of the neuronal responses under the double-cue conditions with attention shifts caused by visual perturbations.
evidence: Direct statement of model performance with reported R² value.

claim: The full model performed significantly better than the reduced models.
source: The full model performed significantly better than the reduced models, suggesting that the model that takes into account that the attention shift correlates with the value difference between the two cues explains the data best (Figure 5—figure supplement 4, and Supplementary file 1, Table 3).
evidence: Model comparison with reference to supplementary figures and tables.

claim: The passive viewing paradigm allowed the researchers to tease apart reward, choice, eye movement and attention.
source: Using a passive viewing paradigm was the key to our experimental design. It allowed us to tease apart reward, choice, eye movement and attention.
evidence: Statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: In the double-cue condition, the OFC neurons did not encode reward expectation.
source: First of all, in the double-cue condition, the reward was chosen randomly. It is clear that the OFC neurons did not encode reward expectation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental design and neural response patterns.

claim: The OFC neurons' responses to a pair of 8-drops-of-juice cues were statistically the same as to the pair of an 8-drops-of-juice cue and a cue associated with no reward.
source: Their responses to a pair of 8-drops-of-juice cues were statistically the same as to the pair of an 8-drops-of-juice cue and a cue associated with no reward (Figure 5A).
evidence: Statement based on comparison of neural responses shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When a visual perturbation was applied to the lower value cue, the expected reward remained the same.
source: Second, when a visual perturbation was applied to the lower value cue, the expected reward remained the same.
evidence: Statement about the experimental design.

claim: The only reasonable explanation for the observed change of OFC neural responses when perturbation was applied to the lower value cue is the shift of attention toward the lower value cue.
source: Thus, the only reasonable explanation for the observed change of OFC neural responses is the shift of attention toward the lower value cue.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental design and observed neural responses.

claim: The findings of the preponderance of OFC neurons encoding the value of chosen item over neurons encoding unchosen values during decision making can be because the activity of these neurons reflected the attention shift toward the chosen item.
source: Thus, the findings of the preponderance of OFC neurons encoding the value of chosen item over neurons encoding unchosen values during decision making (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Padoa-Schioppa, 2013) can be because the activity of these neurons reflected the attention shift toward the chosen item.
evidence: Interpretation of previous findings in light of current results, supported by citations.

claim: The attentional modulation observed in the OFC was most likely due to a bottom-up instead of top-down attention mechanism.
source: The attentional modulation we observed in the OFC was most likely due to a bottom-up instead of top-down attention mechanism.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental design and results.

claim: The strength of attentional modulation was fairly consistent throughout the whole recording part of the experiment.
source: However, we found the strength of attentional modulation to be fairly consistent throughout the whole recording part of the experiment, which lasted 3 and 5 months for monkeys G and D, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Statement based on analysis of modulation strength over time shown in supplementary figure.

claim: In the double-cue condition without visual perturbations, the OFC neurons seem to encode the higher value cue from the very beginning.
source: In the double-cue condition without visual perturbations, the OFC neurons seem to encode the higher value cue from the very beginning.
evidence: Observation based on neural response data.

claim: The current study did not find evidence for an evolving decision in the OFC.
source: We did not find evidence for an evolving decision in the OFC, calling into question whether the value-based decision making occurs in the OFC.
evidence: Statement about the absence of evidence in the current data.

claim: After many months of training, the cues with high values probably gained greater salience than the cues with low values.
source: After many months of training, the cues with high values probably gained greater salience than the cues with low values (Anderson et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculation about the effects of training, supported by citation.

claim: When competing stimuli were presented inside the same receptive field of a neuron in the visual cortex, the neuron's responses to the attended stimulus were more similar to its responses when the attended stimulus was presented alone.
source: When competing stimuli were presented inside the same receptive field of a neuron in the visual cortex, the neuron's responses to the attended stimulus were more similar to its responses when the attended stimulus was presented alone (Chelazzi et al., 1993; Reynolds et al., 1999; Chelazzi et al., 2001; Ghose and Maunsell, 2008; Lee and Maunsell, 2009, 2010; Ni et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about visual cortex findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: When the attended stimulus was the non-preferred stimulus of an MT neuron, its responses still reflected the influence of the non-attended but preferred stimulus.
source: However, when the attended stimulus was the non-preferred stimulus of an MT neuron, its responses still reflected the influence of the non-attended but preferred stimulus (Ni et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about MT neuron behavior supported by citation.

claim: The current results showed that even the negatively tuned OFC neurons' responses were completely dominated by higher value cues, which were their non-preferred stimuli.
source: In contrast, our results showed that even the negatively tuned OFC neurons' responses were completely dominated by higher value cues, which were their non-preferred stimuli.
evidence: Statement contrasting current findings with previous visual cortex findings.

claim: The normalization models proposed for the visual system in previous studies do not explain the behavior of OFC neurons.
source: Thus, the normalization models proposed for the visual system in the previous studies of the visual cortex do not explain the behavior of OFC neurons.
evidence: Inference drawn from the comparison of OFC and visual cortex neuron behaviors.

claim: The weighting in the normalization model is done across time rather than across space.
source: We believe that the weighting is done across the time rather than across the space.
evidence: Interpretation of the normalization model proposed by the authors.

claim: The weights in the normalization model reflect how often attention is directed to an item.
source: The weights reflect how often attention is directed to an item.
evidence: Interpretation of the normalization model proposed by the authors.

claim: At any given time, the attention works in a winner-take-all fashion.
source: At any given time, the attention works in a winner-take-all fashion.
evidence: Interpretation of the attention mechanism based on the data.

claim: The homogenous attentional modulation within the OFC population leads to the belief that the attentional modulation observed in the OFC is inherited from the visual cortex.
source: The homogenous attentional modulation within the OFC population also leads us to believe that the attentional modulation that we observed in the OFC is inherited from the visual cortex.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of attentional modulation.

claim: OFC neurons had lower noise correlations than neurons in the visual cortex.
source: It has been reported that the OFC neurons had lower noise correlations than neurons in the visual cortex (Padoa-Schioppa, 2013; Conen and Padoa-Schioppa, 2015).
evidence: Statement about OFC neuron properties supported by citations.

claim: Attention decreases noise correlation in the visual cortex.
source: Furthermore, It has been found that attention decreases noise correlation in the visual cortex (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009).
evidence: Statement about attention effects in visual cortex supported by citation.

claim: The lower noise correlations between OFC neurons may be expected if they receive inputs from the population of visual neurons that represent attended stimuli.
source: As we showed that the OFC neurons only encoded the value of attended stimuli, the lower noise correlations between the OFC neurons may be expected if they receive inputs from the population of visual neurons that represent attended stimuli.
evidence: Inference connecting current findings with previous observations about noise correlations.

claim: The current results are consistent with the hypothesis that the OFC encodes the value information of one item at a time even when multiple items are presented.
source: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that the OFC encodes the value information of one item at a time even when multiple items are presented.
evidence: Summary statement connecting results to the main hypothesis.

claim: McGinty et al. (2016) found that the value coding in the OFC was highest when the animals were fixating at locations near the cue.
source: McGinty et al. (2016) found that the value coding in the OFC was highest when the animals were fixating at locations near the cue.
evidence: Statement about previous findings supported by citation.

claim: Rich and Wallis (2016) showed that a single OFC population's activity alternated between states associated with the value of available options.
source: Rich and Wallis (2016) showed that a single OFC population's activity alternated between states associated with the value of available options.
evidence: Statement about previous findings supported by citation.

claim: Human subjects solved a multi-cue probabilistic classification task by integrating different numbers of simultaneously presented cues under varying time pressure, suggesting a sequential processing was in play.
source: Finally, it is reported that human subjects solved a multi-cue probabilistic classification task by integrating different numbers of simultaneously presented cues under varying time pressure, suggesting a sequential processing was in play (Oh et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about human behavioral findings supported by citation.

claim: The current evidence supports the hypothesis that the value information is processed in the brain in a sequential manner that is guided by attention and reflected by the OFC activity.
source: Taken together, the current evidence supports the hypothesis that the value information is processed in the brain in a sequential manner that is guided by attention and reflected by the OFC activity.
evidence: Summary statement integrating current and previous findings.

claim: The findings of offer-value neurons in the OFC are potentially compatible with the current study.
source: Yet these findings are potentially compatible with the current study.
evidence: Statement about the compatibility of previous findings with current results.

claim: Value-based decision making may be driven by the value difference between attended and unattended stimuli, which was found to be represented by the neural activity in human vmPFC and ventral striatum.
source: It was shown that value-based decision making may be driven by the value difference between attended and unattended stimuli, which was found to be represented by the neural activity in human vmPFC and ventral striatum (Krajbich et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement about human fMRI findings supported by citations.
